h1: Electrical Panel Upgrade and Replacement in Broward County
intro: When your panel starts showing its age, it usually lets you know. Breakers that trip for no clear reason, a burning smell near the panel, scorch marks around the cover, lights that dim when the air conditioner kicks on, or a hum you have never heard before. Sometimes there is no warning at all, and the first sign is a letter from your insurance company. Here in South Florida, carriers are refusing to cover homes with obsolete panels, and 4-point inspections are failing them every day. A panel is the heart of your electrical system. When it is worn out or unsafe, everything downstream is at risk. We replace it once, we price it right, and we handle the permit and the inspector for you.

definition.heading: What an electrical panel upgrade is
definition.body: An electrical panel upgrade is the removal of your old load center and the installation of a modern one built to today's code. The panel is where power from the utility is divided into the circuits that feed your home or building. Over the years, panels wear out, run short on space, or come from brands that are no longer considered safe. An upgrade replaces the panel, the breakers, and often the connections and grounding that go with it, so the whole system works the way it should. For many South Florida property owners the trigger is insurance, because carriers now decline or drop coverage over outdated equipment. Whatever brings you to it, the result is a service that is safe, current, and insurable again.

symptoms.title: Your insurer or inspector flagged it
symptoms.body: Your carrier sent a notice, or a 4-point inspection called out the panel. In South Florida this is the most common reason people call us. The company will not renew until the equipment is brought up to a modern, insurable standard.

symptoms.title: Breakers trip for no clear reason
symptoms.body: Breakers trip often, or one refuses to reset. A breaker that will not hold is telling you something downstream is wrong, or the breaker itself is worn out. Either way, it is a sign the panel is no longer doing its job.

symptoms.title: You smell burning or see scorch marks
symptoms.body: You notice a burning smell, scorch marks, or discoloration around the panel cover. That is heat where there should be none. It usually means a connection is failing, and it deserves a look before it gets any worse.

symptoms.title: Lights dim when big appliances start
symptoms.body: Lights flicker or dim when the air conditioner or a large appliance turns on. An occasional flicker can be minor, but a steady pattern often points to a panel that can no longer carry the load it is being asked to carry.

symptoms.title: You still have fuses or a full panel
symptoms.body: You still have a fuse box, or the panel is packed and there is no room to add a circuit. Older equipment was built for a lighter electrical life than the one your home lives today. It runs out of room.

symptoms.title: The panel is warm or buzzing
symptoms.body: The panel feels warm to the touch, or you hear a buzz coming from inside it. Electricity is something we do not see, we only feel the effect. Warmth and sound are two effects worth taking seriously before they grow.

localSections.heading: South Florida homes and the panels inside them
localSections.body: Broward County housing was built across many decades, and every era left its own electrical fingerprint. Homes from the middle of the last century often still carry fuse boxes or early breaker panels that were sized for a much lighter electrical life. Homes from later decades frequently hold panel brands that the industry no longer considers safe. Newer construction is generally well protected, which is exactly why the older stock stands out to inspectors and carriers. When you drive through neighborhoods from West Palm Beach down to North Miami, you are looking at panels of every age living side by side. That is not a scare story, it is simply the reality of an area that grew in waves. An upgrade brings an older home's most important piece of equipment up to the standard the rest of the house already expects.

localSections.heading: Heat, humidity, and salt air are hard on equipment
localSections.body: Electrical equipment in South Florida works in a climate that is tough on metal and connections. Constant heat keeps components warm even at rest. Humidity finds its way into enclosures. Homes near the coast deal with salt air that quietly corrodes lugs, bus bars, and the terminations inside a panel. A connection that has slowly loosened or corroded runs hotter than it should, and heat is the enemy of a panel. This is why equipment down here can age faster than the same panel would in a drier, cooler place. When we open a panel during an assessment, the condition of the connections tells us a great deal about how much life is left in it. We factor that reality into the forecast so the upgrade we quote actually holds up in the environment it has to live in.

localSections.heading: Permitting and code reality in Broward
localSections.body: A panel upgrade in Broward County is permitted work, and it should be. The permit is what puts a licensed contractor and a county inspector between you and a mistake that could cost you your home. Electrical code is updated on a multi-year cycle, so a panel that met code when it was installed can fall well behind what today's code requires. When we upgrade a panel we bring it up to the current standard, not the standard from decades ago. We pull the permit, we schedule the inspection, and the owner is the one who meets the inspector on site. That last part matters. The person who priced your job and knows every detail of it is the person standing there when the county signs off, so nothing gets lost in translation.

localSections.heading: Why carriers are driving so many upgrades
localSections.body: The insurance market in South Florida has tightened, and outdated electrical equipment is one of the first things carriers look at. A 4-point inspection reports on the roof, plumbing, HVAC, and electrical, and an obsolete panel is a common reason the electrical section fails. Some carriers decline new policies over it. Others drop existing customers at renewal. This is honest, verifiable reality, and it is why a homeowner who never worried about the panel suddenly has a deadline. We describe it calmly because there is no need to dramatize it. The path forward is straightforward. Replace the equipment with a modern, code-compliant panel, pass the inspection, and the electrical objection goes away. We have walked many South Florida property owners through exactly that, and we can walk you through it too.

guide.title: The complete guide to upgrading your electrical panel in South Florida

sections.heading: What a panel upgrade actually is
sections.body: Your electrical panel is the point where power from the utility enters your property and gets divided into the individual circuits that feed your lights, outlets, and appliances. People call it the panel, the breaker box, the load center, or the fuse box, and they are all talking about the same thing. A panel upgrade is the removal of that old equipment and the installation of a modern replacement built to today's code. Depending on the property, an upgrade can be just the panel itself, or it can include the breakers, the grounding, the connections, and the way the panel ties into the rest of the service. What we replace depends on what we find. The goal is simple: a panel that is the right size for how the property actually uses power, wired with connections that run cool, protected by breakers that trip the moment they are supposed to. When the heart of the system is sound, everything downstream of it is safer. Electricity is something we do not see, we only feel the effect, so the work of a good panel is quiet and invisible. You notice it most when it is missing.

sections.heading: When a panel upgrade becomes mandatory
sections.body: For a long time a tired panel is an annoyance you learn to live with. A breaker that trips when you run the microwave and the toaster together. A few circuits that share more than they should. Then something changes and the upgrade stops being optional. The most common trigger in South Florida is insurance. A 4-point inspection flags the panel, and your carrier tells you the policy will not renew until the equipment is replaced. That turns a someday project into a dated one. The second trigger is safety. When a panel comes from a brand with a documented history of breakers that fail to trip, or when we find heat damage, corrosion, or a failing connection during an assessment, replacement moves from a good idea to the honest recommendation. The third trigger is capacity. If your panel is full and you want to add a circuit, there is simply no room, and forcing more onto tired equipment is not the answer. We will always tell you plainly which of these you are dealing with. If your panel is fine and has years left, we will tell you that too. We stay in our lane and we do not sell work that does not need doing.

sections.heading: What the day of the work looks like
sections.body: A panel replacement is a focused, one-visit job for our crew in most homes. It is an in and out type of situation. That is what we do. We start by coordinating with the utility so power to the property can be interrupted safely for the work window. Then our in-house crew removes the old panel, sets the new one, and reconnects every circuit, labeling as we go so you end up with a panel you can actually read. We check and correct the grounding and the terminations, because a new panel is only as good as the connections feeding it. Because the same crew does this work day in and day out, there is a rhythm to it, and the property is left clean. You will be without power for part of the day, and we tell you honestly ahead of time what to expect so you can plan around it. Once the work is complete, we schedule the county inspection. When you hire a crew with ten years of situations already behind them, the day of the work tends to hold few surprises, and that is the whole point. Before we arrive, you do not need to do much beyond clearing a little space around the panel and making a plan for the hours the power will be down. If you work from home or rely on medical equipment, tell us up front so we can schedule the window around your needs. We would rather build the day around your life than ask you to build your life around us.

sections.heading: An honest conversation about cost
sections.body: A panel upgrade is quoted per property after an on-site assessment, and there is a good reason we do not post a flat price. The number depends on the condition of the existing service, the grounding, the size the property needs, and what we uncover when we open things up. Two houses on the same street can carry very different jobs behind the panel cover. Our service call is $240, which covers roughly two hours including travel, arrival, and diagnosis, and if the problem can be handled on the spot there is no separate return charge. When the work is a full replacement, we forecast what the job actually takes and we give you one price before we begin. That price does not change mid-job. We do not come back partway through with new fees. Price it once, price it right. If a panel upgrade is part of a larger electrical service rebuild, we will show you where the line is and quote that scope honestly as well. Losing an honestly priced bid is fine with us. What we will not do is win a job with a low number and make it up later. That is not how we work, and it never has been. If a panel upgrade turns out to be part of a larger service rebuild, we will show you exactly where one job ends and the other begins, and we will price each scope on its own so you can see what you are paying for. There is never a reason to bundle in things you do not need to reach a number you cannot read. Clear pricing is part of treating you like family, and it is how we have kept customers coming back and sending their neighbors for ten years.

sections.heading: How to choose the right contractor
sections.body: A panel sits at the center of your home's safety, so the person who replaces it matters as much as the panel itself. Start with licensing. Ask whether the contractor holds a real state license and can pull a permit in their own name. Ghost Crown Electric is a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor with statewide authority and a Broward County Master Electrician, with 286 permitted projects on public record. Ask who actually does the work. A rotating crew of subcontractors is not the same as an in-house team that has worked together for years. Ask whether the owner attends the inspection. When the person who priced the job is the person who meets the inspector, details do not fall through the cracks. Ask how they price. A contractor who forecasts the job and holds the number is telling you they understand the work. And be careful of anyone who wins by talking down every other company. We do not do that. We stay in our lane, we let the license and the record speak, and we give a customer more than what they pay for. That is a better sign than any sales pitch.

sections.heading: Why insurance is reshaping panels across South Florida
sections.body: It is worth understanding the wave that is bringing so many people to this page, because it helps to know you are not alone and nothing about your situation is unusual. Over recent years the South Florida insurance market has tightened, and carriers have grown far stricter about the condition of the properties they cover. Electrical equipment is near the top of the list they scrutinize. The 4-point inspection is the mechanism. It looks at four systems, and the electrical portion routinely fails when the panel is an obsolete brand or is simply worn out. A failed 4-point can mean a declined new policy or a dropped renewal on a home you have insured for years. None of this is a reflection on you as an owner. It is a market correcting for risk, and the risk it is worried about is real. The steady, unglamorous fix is to replace the equipment with a modern panel, pass the inspection, and remove the objection. We handle the replacement and the permit, and the owner meets the inspector so the sign-off is clean. Then the electrical reason your policy was in question is gone.

sections.heading: What we do and what we leave alone
sections.body: We want to be clear about our lane, because knowing what a company does not do is as useful as knowing what it does. We upgrade and replace electrical panels and distribution equipment for homes and commercial properties across our service area, from West Palm Beach down to North Miami and through the Broward County core. When a panel is part of a larger job, we handle full electrical service rebuilds, meter equipment, and the grounding and surge protection that go with a modern service. Proper grounding is not a gimmick. It protects your family, your home, and your investment as a whole, and it is part of doing a panel right. What we will not do is oversell you. If your existing panel is a safe, current brand with room to spare, we are not going to talk you into replacing it. We show up when we say we will, we tell you the truth about what your equipment needs, and we do the work in front of us with care. That is the whole job, and we take all of it seriously.

faqs.question: My insurance company flagged my panel. What now?
faqs.answer: Send us the notice or the 4-point report and we will read it with you. In most cases the fix is a modern, code-compliant panel that passes inspection. We come out, assess the service in person, quote the replacement per property, pull the permit, and the owner meets the inspector so the sign-off is clean and your carrier's objection goes away.

faqs.question: Do I really need a permit for this?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you want one. A permit puts a licensed contractor and a county inspector between you and a costly mistake, and it documents that the work was done to current code. We pull the permit as part of the job, schedule the inspection, and the owner personally meets the inspector on site, so nothing about the sign-off is left to chance.

faqs.question: Will my power be off during the work?
faqs.answer: For part of the day, yes. Replacing a panel means the power feeding it has to be interrupted safely while we work. We tell you honestly ahead of time what to expect so you can plan around it, and because our in-house crew does this work constantly, it is a focused, in and out type of situation rather than a job that drags on.

faqs.question: Is my old panel actually dangerous, or is this overselling?
faqs.answer: It depends on what we find. Some panels come from brands with a documented history of breakers that fail to trip, and those we recommend replacing plainly. Others are simply worn or full. If your panel is a safe, current brand with life left in it, we will tell you that and leave it alone. We stay in our lane and only recommend work that needs doing.

faqs.question: How long does a panel upgrade take?

We will give you a realistic window when we quote the work, and we will not promise a specific timeline before we have seen the service in person. Every electrical situation is a little different, and the site visit comes first.
